strengths: Clear and elegant theoretical contribution: Theorem 4.1 provides a clean decomposition of MI into drift differences, soundly grounded in diffusion theory

Incremental technical novelty: The method primarily applies existing conditional bridge matching (Shi et al., 2023) to MI estimation; Theorem 4.1 is a straightforward application of standard tools
High computational cost (6-18 GPU-hours per run on A100) not adequately discussed or compared to alternatives like MINDE; requires 100k training samples

strengths: Novel and elegant theoretical contribution: Theorem 4.1 provides a creative decomposition of MI into differences of diffusion drifts using reciprocal processes, with mathematically sound proof
Unbiased estimator property: Unlike MINDE which has unavoidable bias, InfoBridge is theoretically unbiased under perfect drift approximation
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Extensive benchmarking with 40+ low-dimensional tests and multiple high-dimensional image benchmarks against 11+ baselines
Clear mathematical exposition: Well-presented background on reciprocal processes and bridge matching theory, making complex concepts accessible
Practical algorithmic insight: Using single neural network with binary input for drift approximation reduces approximation errors intelligently
Generalizability: Framework naturally extends to KL divergence, differential entropy, pointwise MI, and interaction information estimation
Thorough supplementary materials: Detailed experimental procedures, hyperparameters, and additional ablations in appendix
weaknesses: Inconsistent empirical improvements: Performance on low-dimensional benchmarks is identical to MINDE; on 32×32 images, InfoBridge underperforms MIENF/AE+WKL; confidence intervals frequently overlap with baselines
Limited practical algorithm novelty: Core learning procedure simply applies existing conditional bridge matching via standard regression; algorithmic contribution is incremental

Significant practical limitations: (1) Fixed 100k training data requirement without sensitivity analysis, (2) Failure on heavy-tailed distributions (Cauchy), (3) High computational cost (6-18 GPU-hours/run) without complexity analysis, (4) Critical hyperparameter ε fixed at 1 with no sensitivity study
Missing crucial ablations: No ablation on ε sensitivity, binary conditioning design, neural architecture choices, or convergence rate analysis under finite-sample approximation

Gap between theory and practice: Unbiased property emphasized but finite-sample convergence rates and approximation error analysis not provided; unclear how to balance theoretical unbiasedness against practical approximation errors

Questionable comparison fairness: Claims of being 'bias-free best estimator' are narrow—methods that outperform InfoBridge (MIENF, AE+WKL) don't fit this category; using 100k samples vs. unknown amounts for baselines
Limited practical guidance: No principled method for setting ε, no guidance on when to use InfoBridge vs. MINDE vs. MIENF, no investigation of performance degradation with fewer samples
Underexplored byproducts: Sampling from learned conditional distributions mentioned but not evaluated; sample quality assessment would strengthen claims

Competitive performance with MINDE on low-dimensional and image benchmarks without requiring inductive bias assumptions, unlike AE+WKL methods

Excellent reproducibility with detailed descriptions of neural network architectures, training procedures, and hyperparameter choices
weaknesses: Critical gap between theory and practice: Theorem 4.1 establishes an unbiased decomposition, but the practical algorithm (Algorithm 2) uses learned neural networks that introduce significant bias; this approximation error is not rigorously analyzed

Limited algorithmic novelty: the practical algorithm is straightforward application of existing conditional bridge matching; the contribution is recognizing the MI decomposition, not developing new techniques

Volatility parameter ε requires problem-dependent tuning without principled selection guidelines; Tables 2-3 show optimal ε varies by orders of magnitude (0.001 to 10), contradicting robustness claims
